_comment: Guided tour: align vs super, on 1DG3 and 1F5N -- human guanylate binding protein-1 nucleotide-free and with a GTP analogue. The same protein in two states, so the superposition has a meaning (what moved) rather than being an exercise. Steps point at real controls and wait for the user to run the command. Read by chimol.tour.
title: Superpose two structures: align, super, rms

steps.title: The same protein, twice
steps.text:
1DG3 and 1F5N are human guanylate binding protein-1: nucleotide-free, and bound to a GTP analogue. Superposing them is not an exercise -- it is how you see what binding moved.

Eight steps. You run the commands; the tour points at where they go.

steps.title: Load the first
steps.text: The nucleotide-free form. It will be the target: the structure that stays put, with the other moved onto it.

steps.title: And the second
steps.text: The GTP-analogue complex. Both arrive in their own deposited frames, which have nothing to do with each other -- so at this point the two are somewhere in space together and the picture means nothing yet.
steps.hint: Type fetch 1F5N, then zoom all to see both.

steps.title: Tell them apart first
steps.text: Two structures in one colour cannot be compared. Colour them separately before superposing anything, or the result is a single tangle that always looks like it worked.

steps.title: align: match the sequences, then superpose
steps.text: align pairs residues by identity -- chain and residue number where they agree, and a sequence alignment where they do not -- and then finds the rotation that minimises the distance between the pairs. Pairing by position in the selection instead is a classic silent error: a structure missing one loop pairs every later residue against its neighbour and returns a confident, meaningless number. Watch the report: it says how many residues were paired out of how many.
steps.hint: Type align 1f5n, 1dg3. Note the RMSD and the residue count.

steps.title: super: when the sequences do not help
steps.text: super does the same job without trusting the sequence, refining the set of matched pairs by rejecting outliers over several cycles. It is what you use for two structures that fold the same way but do not share a sequence -- and, here, for a second opinion. If the two RMSDs disagree a lot, the pairing is what differs, not the geometry.
steps.hint: Type super 1f5n, 1dg3 and compare the number with align's.

steps.title: rms: measure without moving anything
steps.text: rms reports the deviation where the structures already are. Run after a superposition it is the fit's own residual; run before one it tells you how far apart the deposited frames were. It pairs residues by identity too, and then matches the atoms by name inside each paired residue -- two structures need not carry the same atoms per residue, and lining up two flat atom lists by position is the same mistake one level down.

steps.title: Now look at what moved
steps.text: With the two superposed, the differences are the point. Colour by the deviation, or simply look: the domain that closes around the nucleotide is what this pair is famous for. align also leaves the pairing behind it, so the sequence strip shows which residues were matched and which had no partner.
steps.hint: Type zoom 1f5n and compare the two chains where they diverge.
